newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK's Clarke pledges tax cuts, rates unchanged.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK's Clarke pledges tax cuts, rates unchanged.

text.p: British finance minister Kenneth Clarke left official interest rates unchanged on Thursday and repeated a pledge to bring the country's basic rate of tax down to 20 percent as soon as public finances allowed.
"I have been absolutely clear that my target of taxation is to reach a standard rate of 20 pence in the pound and it will be achieved as long as public finances can afford it," he said.

At a news conference spearheading the ruling Conservative Party's autumn campaign for next year's general election, Clarke fiercly defended his decision to raise taxes in the first few budgets he presided over as Chancellor of the Exchequer.
"Yes, we took tough measures which involved some increases in taxation. We will continue on that tax cutting agenda when it is sensible to do so," he said.
Income tax cuts in last year's budget for fiscal 1996/7, the first for seven years, reduced the basic rate of tax by one penny in the pound to 24 percent. The starting rate is 20 pence.
Most economists expect the embattled government to cut taxes by between two and three billion pounds in this year's budget as part of its efforts to woo back a disgruntled electorate.
The unspectacular offering -- which many economists think is unwarranted given the government's heavy debt burden -- will undoubtedly be offset by spending cuts, the same as last year.

Clarke said reducing the basic rate of income tax to 20 pence in the pound for all the people paying 24 pence now would cost the country around 7.0 billion pounds ($10.98 billion). He dismissed a pledge from the opposition Labour Party to cut the starting rate of tax to ten or 15 percent as "incredible".

"Labour cannot and will not say no to raising the basic rate, raising the higher rate, or introducing a new top rate. As night follows day, the tax burden would rise, if Britain ever elected a Labour government," Clarke said.

The Conservatives have been in power for 17 years, but for many months opinion polls have shown them trailing the Labour Party by more than 20 percentage points. The next general election must take place by May 1997 at the latest.
Clarke claimed Labour would destroy his efforts to get and keep the economy in a sustainable recovery with low inflation, low interest rates and falling unemployment.

Meanwhile the Bank of England operated at unchanged dealing rates in the domestic money market, confirming Clarke had decided to leave official base rates unchanged at 5-3/4 percent at Wednesday's monthly monetary meeting.

Many economists believe that another rate cut is still on the cards, but said that for the moment the Bank's caution against igniting inflation pressures had overcome any temptation Clarke may have had to loosen monetary policy.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said in a trades survey released on Thursday that annual retail sales rose once again in August, with the balance of firms reporting a rise in sales the largest since November 1988.
It welcomed Clarke's decision to leave interest rates unchanged for now and said there was no need for a rate rise.
"That's exactly what we like to see. There's no need to fear an increase in inflation yet. We're certainly not seeing 1980s style boom conditions," said Alastair Eperon, head of the CBI survey panel.

In a document aimed at revealing implicit tax rises concealed in recent policy statements from the Labour Party, Clarke said that since the last general election in 1992, the average British family had 750 pounds ($1,175) more to spend.
